attempts: Validation of canonical integer format: The regex /^[1-9][0-9]*$/ correctly rejects all non-canonical forms (leading zero, negative sign, plus sign, decimal, exponent, surrounding whitespace) and returns 400 with { "error": "invalid limit" }.
Safe integer boundary enforcement: Number.isSafeInteger check rejects values beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (tested with 20-digit value returning 400), ensuring no out-of-range integers are accepted.

Array parameter rejection from repeated keys: When Express parses ?limit=1&limit=2 as an array, typeof check correctly identifies it as non-string and returns 400, blocking the repeated-parameter attack.
ReDoS via `/^[1-9][0-9]*$/` regex pattern - simple anchored pattern with no nested quantifiers, fails fast on non-matches
Integer overflow via Number.isSafeInteger bypass - code correctly validates with Number.isSafeInteger() check rejecting numbers beyond JavaScript safe range per spec ac-9
Repeated query parameter array injection `?limit=1&limit=2` - code checks `typeof raw !== 'string'` before regex, rejecting arrays per spec ac-10
Non-canonical integer formats (01, 0, -1, 1.5, 1e1, +1) - regex `/^[1-9][0-9]*$/` rejects all non-canonical forms per spec ac-8
State mutation on validation failure per spec ac-11 - validation checks precede all state access, early return on invalid input leaves items Map and nextId untouched
Parameter scope leakage per spec ac-13 - limit validation is scoped to GET /items handler only; other routes never check req.query.limit
Sensitive data exposure - error response matches spec exactly as `{ error: 'invalid limit' }` with no user input reflection or state leakage
Bypass canonical positive integer validation with leading zero (limit=01): blocked by regex [1-9] requirement, verified by ac-8 test passing with 400 rejection
Cause integer overflow using large number beyond MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (limit=99999999999999999999): blocked by Number.isSafeInteger() check, verified by ac-9 test passing with 400 rejection
Confuse parser with repeated limit parameters (limit=1&limit=2 parsed as array): blocked by typeof raw !== 'string' check, verified by ac-10 test passing with 400 rejection

attempts: Verify plain code-unit string comparison (ac-4): items sorted as 'Apple, Zebra, apple, banana' using JavaScript's < operator on code units (65, 90, 97, 98 respectively), matching spec exactly.

Repeated sort parameter attack: send ?sort=name&sort=id to exploit array parsing. Express parses as array ['name', 'id']. The validation check (sort !== 'name' && sort !== 'id') correctly rejects arrays and returns 400.

Case-sensitivity bypass: send ?sort=Name or ?sort=ID. The code uses exact string comparison (sort !== 'name'), so case variants fail validation and return 400 as specified in acceptance criteria ac-8.

Prototype pollution via sort parameter: send ?sort=__proto__ or ?sort=constructor. The strict validation (sort !== 'name' && sort !== 'id') rejects both, preventing any property access or object manipulation. Blocked safely with 400.

Attempt 1: Remove the validation check on line 24. If I delete the condition checking sort !== undefined && sort !== 'name' && sort !== 'id', then invalid sort values like 'created', '', 'Name', and arrays would be accepted instead of returning 400, causing ac-6, ac-7, ac-8, ac-9 tests to fail on their 400 status assertions.

Attempt 2: Break code-unit comparison by using case-insensitive sorting on line 37. If I change the comparator to a.name.toLowerCase() < b.name.toLowerCase(), uppercase and lowercase letters would sort together instead of having all uppercase ASCII before lowercase ASCII, causing ac-4 test to fail its assertion that order is Apple, Zebra, apple, banana.

Attempt 3: Mutate the items store during sorting on line 37. If I insert items.clear() or modify items before calling res.json(result), then ac-10 would fail because the subsequent unsorted fetch would show the store was mutated instead of remaining unchanged, and ac-3 would fail if state persisted.
